title: CSC2770 Module 2 — Tour of Computer Systems

questions.q: The module's diagram shows main memory holding both "Instructions (Programs)" and "Data". What design idea does this reflect?
choices: The stored-program (von Neumann) concept: programs are data kept in the same memory as the values they operate on
The Harvard architecture: instructions and data have separate memories
The memory hierarchy: instructions are faster than data
Virtual memory: each program sees its own private memory
questions.explain: In a **von Neumann** machine, instructions and data share one memory (and one path to it), so loading a new program is just loading more data. The **Harvard** alternative uses separate instruction and data memories/buses.

questions.q: What is the **von Neumann bottleneck**?
choices: Because instructions and data share one path to memory, the CPU often has to wait on memory
The CPU can only run one process at a time
The ALU can only perform one operation per clock cycle
Registers are too few to hold a whole program
questions.explain: A single shared path for both instruction fetches and data accesses means the fast CPU spends time waiting for the slower memory. Caches (and split L1i/L1d caches) exist largely to soften this.

questions.q: Modern PCs are often described as "modified Harvard". What does that mean?
choices: Main memory is unified (von Neumann), but the fastest cache level is split into separate instruction and data caches
Instructions are stored on disk and data in RAM
There are two separate CPUs, one for instructions and one for data
Main memory is split into an instruction RAM and a data RAM on separate buses
questions.explain: The big DRAM is shared by code and data (von Neumann), while **L1 is split into L1i and L1d**, which lets the fetch stage and the LSU access cache at the same time (Harvard-like).

questions.q: Which best describes an **instruction set architecture (ISA)**?
choices: The complete set of instructions a CPU understands, plus its registers and the rules for encoding instructions as bits
The physical layout of transistors on the CPU die
The operating system's list of system calls
The programming language a compiler accepts
questions.explain: The ISA is the hardware/software contract: instructions, registers and encodings. x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V are different ISAs, which is why machine code for one won't run on another.

questions.q: An instruction is a binary number divided into fields. What does the **opcode** field specify?
choices: *What* operation to perform
Which registers or memory address the operation uses
The address of the next instruction
How many clock cycles the instruction takes
questions.explain: The **opcode** says *what* to do (add, load, branch...). The other fields name the **operands**: registers, a memory address or a constant.

questions.q: RISC-V has 32 registers. How many bits does each register field in an instruction need to name any one of them?
questions.explain: *n* bits can name 2^n things. 2^5 = 32, so each of rd, rs1 and rs2 is a 5-bit field.

questions.q: A hypothetical ISA has **1,024** registers. How many bits would each register-name field in an instruction require?
questions.explain: 2^10 = 1,024, so 10 bits per register field. This is one reason large register files are impractical: every instruction naming three registers would spend 30 bits just on register names.

questions.q: In the RISC-V R-type encoding of `add x5, x6, x7` (x5 ← x6 + x7), which field holds `00101`?
choices: rd (destination register)
rs1 (source register 1)
rs2 (source register 2)
opcode
questions.explain: `00101` = 5, i.e. **x5**, the destination. rs1 = `00110` (x6), rs2 = `00111` (x7), and the opcode `0110011` means register-to-register arithmetic, with funct3/funct7 narrowing it to ADD.

questions.q: In RISC-V, `add` and `sub` share the same opcode field value; they are distinguished by the funct7 field (`0000000` for ADD, `0100000` for SUB).
questions.explain: The 7-bit opcode `0110011` just says "register-register arithmetic". The funct3 and funct7 fields pick the specific operation, so ADD and SUB differ only in funct7.

questions.q: What are the three phases of the instruction cycle, in order?
choices: Fetch, decode, execute
Decode, fetch, execute
Load, compute, store
Fetch, execute, write back
questions.explain: The CPU repeats **fetch → decode → execute** from power-on to power-off. Finer textbook models (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) are refinements of this.

questions.q: Which component performs the **fetch** of an instruction?
choices: The Control Unit
The Load-Store Unit
The ALU
The cache controller
questions.explain: Fetch is **CU work**: the CU puts the PC's address on the address bus and READ on the control bus. The LSU only handles memory accesses that are part of *executing* an instruction.

questions.q: What happens during the **decode** phase?
choices: The Control Unit interprets the bits in the IR and generates control signals for the other components
The instruction is read from memory over the data bus
The ALU computes the result
The PC is loaded with the reset vector
questions.explain: Decode is internal to the CPU: the CU splits the IR into opcode and operand fields and turns them into control signals (register selects, ALU opcode, write enables). No system-bus traffic.

questions.q: Which of the following **use the system bus**? Select all that apply.
choices: Fetching an instruction
Decoding an instruction
Executing `LOAD R1, [0x200]`
Executing `ADD R3, R1, R2`
Executing `STORE R3, [0x208]`
questions.explain: Fetch uses the bus (CU). Decode is internal. Execute uses the bus **only** if the instruction reads or writes memory (LSU): loads and stores do, a register-only ADD doesn't (ignoring cache hits, which avoid the bus).

questions.q: Which statement about the Control Unit is correct?
choices: It doesn't compute results itself; it tells the other components what to do and when
It performs all arithmetic that the ALU cannot
It stores the operands for the current instruction
It holds the address of the next instruction
questions.explain: The CU is the "conductor": it manages the fetch-decode-execute cycle and generates control signals. Computing is the ALU's job; operands live in registers; the address of the next instruction is in the PC.

questions.q: For `ADD R3, R1, R2`, which set of signals would the CU generate during decode?
choices: Register file: output R1 and R2 to the ALU; ALU: use opcode ADD; register file: write the ALU output into R3 at the next clock edge
Address bus ← R1; control bus ← READ; data bus → R3
LSU: load R1 and R2 from memory, then store R3
PC ← R3; IR ← R1 + R2
questions.explain: An ADD is register-only, so the CU steers the register file (which to read, which to write) and the ALU (which operation). No bus or LSU involvement.

questions.q: How does **microprogrammed** control differ from **hardwired** control?
choices: Each machine instruction triggers a sequence of micro-instructions stored in an on-chip control store; it is flexible but slower
It uses software in RAM to decode instructions
It maps opcode bits straight to control signals with fixed logic; it is fast but hard to change
It is only used in GPUs
questions.explain: **Hardwired** = fixed combinational logic from opcode to signals (fast, typical of RISC). **Microprogrammed** = a small ROM of micro-instructions per machine instruction (flexible, historically CISC/x86). Modern x86 mostly uses hardwired decoders into micro-ops and falls back to microcode for complex instructions.

questions.q: How can a pipelined CPU finish close to one instruction per clock cycle even though each instruction takes several cycles?
choices: Different instructions occupy different stages at once: while one executes, the next is decoded and the one after that fetched
It skips the decode phase for simple instructions
It runs the clock several times faster during execute
It executes every instruction in the ALU in a single gate delay
questions.explain: Pipelining is like an assembly line: each stage works on a different instruction simultaneously, so throughput approaches one instruction per cycle even though **latency** per instruction is several cycles.

questions.q: The slides list "switching between processes" as ordinary CPU work. What does a **context switch** mainly consist of?
choices: Saving one process's registers and PC to memory and loading another process's saved registers and PC
Copying the whole program from disk into cache
Rebooting the CPU with a new reset vector
Clearing main memory so the next process starts clean
questions.explain: A process's CPU state is its register contents including the PC. The OS (usually on a timer interrupt) stores those to memory and loads another's, which is just loads and stores of register contents.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
choices: PC holds an **address** (where the next instruction is); IR holds an **instruction** (the bits being decoded/executed)
PC holds the current instruction; IR holds the address of the next instruction
PC holds the result of the last ALU operation; IR holds the instruction count
Both hold addresses: PC for instructions, IR for data
questions.explain: Classic confusion. **PC = address**, e.g. `0x00400108`; **IR = instruction bits**, e.g. `0x007302B3` (`add x5, x6, x7`). Fetch reads memory at PC into IR, then advances PC.

questions.q: A register contains `0x007302B3`, which is the encoding of `add x5, x6, x7`. Which register is it most likely to be, during decode?
choices: The Instruction Register
The Program Counter
The Stack Pointer
The flags register
questions.explain: It's an instruction's bit pattern, so it's in the **IR**. The PC would hold the *address* where the next instruction is stored.

questions.q: On a machine with fixed 4-byte instructions, the instruction at address `0x10C` is fetched. What is the PC afterwards, in decimal? (0x10C = 268)
questions.explain: Sequential execution: PC ← PC + 4. `0x10C` + 4 = `0x110` = 272. The PC advances right after fetch, before the instruction executes.

questions.q: By the time an instruction executes, the PC already points at the *next* instruction.
questions.explain: The PC is incremented immediately after fetch. That's why many machines compute branch targets relative to "PC + instruction size".

questions.q: Why can't an x86-64 CPU simply do `PC ← PC + 4` after every fetch?
choices: x86-64 instructions vary from 1 to 15 bytes, so the increment depends on the instruction just fetched
x86-64 has no program counter
x86-64 always branches after every instruction
x86-64 instructions are 8 bytes each
questions.explain: RISC-V and ARM64 use (almost) fixed 4-byte instructions. x86-64 is variable-length (1-15 bytes), so the PC (called RIP on x86) advances by the fetched instruction's length.

questions.q:
In this loop, what happens when R1 becomes 0?

```
0x100: SUB R1, R1, #1
0x104: BNZ 0x100   ; branch if Zero flag == 0
0x108: ...
```
choices: SUB sets the Zero flag, BNZ doesn't branch, and the PC's normal increment to `0x108` stands
BNZ sets PC ← 0x100 and the loop continues forever
The CPU halts because R1 is zero
The PC is reset to the reset vector
questions.explain: A conditional branch sets PC ← target **only if** its condition holds; otherwise the incremented PC stands. When R1 hits 0, Z = 1, so "branch if not zero" falls through to `0x108`.

questions.q: What does a function **call** instruction do to the PC?
choices: It saves the return address (the incremented PC), e.g. by pushing it on the stack, then sets the PC to the function's address
It increments the PC by the function's size
It copies the function's code into the IR
It sets the PC to the reset vector
questions.explain: A call is a jump that remembers where to come back to. A **return** pops the saved address back into the PC.

questions.q: What is the PC's **reset vector**?
choices: The fixed, usually hardwired address the PC holds at power-on, pointing into firmware
The address of the most recently executed instruction
An interrupt that resets the ALU flags
The first address of the operating system kernel in RAM
questions.explain: At power-on the CPU must start somewhere fixed, so the reset vector is built into it. On x86 it is `0xFFFFFFF0`, where the motherboard maps the firmware flash chip.

questions.q: Why must the reset vector point into firmware in non-volatile memory rather than into RAM?
choices: RAM is volatile, so at power-on it holds no program to run
RAM is too slow to fetch the first instruction
The PC cannot hold RAM addresses
The OS forbids the CPU from reading RAM before boot
questions.explain: Main memory loses everything without power. The only code available at power-on is the firmware (BIOS/UEFI) stored in flash/ROM, which initializes hardware and loads the bootloader and OS into RAM.

questions.q: Put the boot chain in order: (1) bootloader loads the kernel, (2) PC = reset vector, (3) firmware runs POST and finds a boot device, (4) kernel starts user programs.
questions.explain: Reset → PC = reset vector → firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs **POST**, initializes hardware, loads a **bootloader** → bootloader loads the **kernel** into RAM and jumps to it → kernel starts user programs.

questions.q: Which of these is a **general-purpose** register's job?
choices: Holding operands and intermediate results chosen by the program/compiler
Holding the address of the next instruction
Holding the instruction currently being decoded
Holding the ALU's Zero/Negative/Overflow flags
questions.explain: **GPRs** hold data values for computation. The PC, IR and status/flags register are **special-purpose registers** with dedicated jobs.

questions.q: Which of these are **special-purpose registers**? Select all that apply.
choices: Program Counter
Instruction Register
Status/flags register
A register the compiler uses for a loop counter
questions.explain: PC, IR, the flags register (and the stack pointer, MAR/MDR in textbook models) have dedicated roles. A register chosen by the compiler to hold a loop counter is a GPR.

questions.q: Registers are faster to access than cache or main memory because they are located directly in the CPU.
questions.explain: Registers sit in the CPU core next to the ALU and are read/written within a single clock cycle (well under a nanosecond).

questions.q: Registers are built from flip-flops. What kind of circuit does that make them?
choices: Sequential: their output depends on stored state, captured at clock edges
Combinational: their output depends only on current inputs
Analog: they store a continuous voltage
Volatile ROM
questions.explain: Flip-flops hold a bit via feedback and capture input on a clock edge, so registers are **sequential**. The ALU, by contrast, is **combinational**.

questions.q: What does calling a CPU "64-bit" mean?
choices: Its GPRs (and addresses) are 64 bits wide, so it can operate on 64-bit integers in one instruction and in principle address 2^64 bytes
It has 64 general-purpose registers
It runs at 64 GHz
Its cache lines are 64 bytes
questions.explain: Word size is the width of the GPRs. A 32-bit CPU has 32-bit registers and a 2^32-byte (4 GiB) address space. (Cache lines being 64 bytes is a coincidence of numbers.)

questions.q: Where do the ALU's inputs come from?
choices: The operands come from registers; the operation comes as a control signal from the most recently decoded instruction
Both operands and the operation are read directly from main memory
The operands come from the PC and IR
The operation is chosen by the ALU based on its last result
questions.explain: Per the slides: operands from **registers**, operation (opcode) from the **CU's decode** of the current instruction.

questions.q: Why is the ALU called a **combinational** circuit?
choices: It has no internal memory; its output depends only on its current inputs, not on previous inputs
It combines several instructions into one
It combines the CPU and memory into one chip
It can only do operations that combine two operands
questions.explain: The ALU is a pure function f(A, B, op). It doesn't remember the last result, so the result must be captured in a register at a clock edge.

questions.q: Why does the combinational ALU make a clock necessary?
choices: Its output flickers through intermediate values while signals propagate; the clock edge marks when registers capture the settled result
Without a clock the ALU would forget its opcode table
The clock supplies the power the ALU runs on
The clock tells the ALU which operation to perform
questions.explain: When inputs change, the output settles after gate delays (e.g. rippling carries). Edge-triggered registers capture only at the edge, and the period is chosen longer than the slowest path, so only correct, stable values are stored.

questions.q: The example ALU uses a 2-bit opcode. How many distinct operations can a **5-bit** opcode select?
questions.explain: *n* opcode bits select 2^n operations: 2^5 = 32. The example's 2 bits select exactly 4 (ADD 00, SUB 01, NOT 10, NEG 11); real ALUs use 4-8 bits (16-256 operations).

questions.q: In the module's example ALU, what operation does opcode `10` select?
choices: NOT
NEG
SUB
ADD
questions.explain: The table: ADD `00`, SUB `01`, **NOT `10`**, NEG `11`.

questions.q: For Input A = `00000101` (5), what are the outputs of **NOT** and **NEG**?
choices: Both give `11111011`
questions.explain: **NOT** flips every bit (one's complement). **NEG** is two's-complement negation: flip every bit *and add 1*. So NEG x = NOT x + 1.

questions.q: Give the 8-bit output of the example ALU for opcode `10` (NOT) with Input A = `01010000`. Answer as 8 binary digits.
questions.explain: NOT is bitwise complement: `01010000` → `10101111` (−81 as signed). Input B is ignored because NOT is unary.

questions.q: Give the 8-bit output of the example ALU for opcode `11` (NEG) with Input A = `01010000` (80). Answer as 8 binary digits.
questions.explain: NEG = NOT A + 1 = `10101111` + 1 = `10110000`, which is −80 in two's complement.

questions.q: The 8-bit ALU computes ADD with A = `01010000` (80) and B = `00110000` (48). What are the result and flags?
choices: `10000000`; Overflow = 1, Negative = 1, Zero = 0
`10000000`; Overflow = 0, Negative = 0, Zero = 0
`00000000`; Overflow = 1, Zero = 1
`10000000`; Carry = 1, Overflow = 0
questions.explain: 80 + 48 = 128, which exceeds the signed 8-bit max of 127. The bit pattern `10000000` reads as −128: two positives gave a negative, so **V = 1**. The top bit is 1, so **N = 1**. No carry out of bit 7, so C = 0 (unsigned 128 is correct).

questions.q: The example ALU computes SUB (opcode `01`) with A = 80 and B = 48. What is the output as a signed decimal number?
questions.explain: A − B = A + NEG B. NEG 48 = `11010000`. `01010000 + 11010000 = 1 00100000`; drop the 9th bit → `00100000` = 32. Z = 0, N = 0, V = 0 (operands of opposite sign can't overflow).

questions.q: The ALU computes SUB with A = 5, B = 7. Which flags are set?
questions.explain: 5 − 7 = 5 + (−7) = `00000101 + 11111001 = 11111110` = −2. The top bit is 1 so **N = 1**. Adding operands of opposite sign can never overflow, so V = 0.

questions.q: ADD −1 + 1 in 8 bits: `11111111 + 00000001 = 1 00000000`. Which flags result?
questions.explain: The 8-bit result is all zeros (**Z = 1**) and a bit carried out of the top (**C = 1**, unsigned overflow: 255 + 1). But as signed, −1 + 1 = 0 is correct, so **V = 0**. Carry tracks unsigned overflow; Overflow tracks signed overflow.

questions.q: Adding a positive and a negative two's-complement number can never cause signed overflow.
questions.explain: The result's magnitude is at most the larger operand's, so it always fits. Overflow in addition happens only when both operands have the **same** sign and the result has the opposite sign.

questions.q: What happens when the 8-bit ALU performs NEG on `10000000` (−128)?
choices: The result is `10000000` (−128 again) and Overflow = 1, because +128 can't be represented
The result is `01111111` (+127) with no flags
The result is `00000000` with Zero = 1
The result is `10000001` (−127)
questions.explain: NOT `10000000` = `01111111`, + 1 = `10000000`. The 8-bit signed range is −128 to +127, so +128 doesn't exist; this is the one negation that overflows.

questions.q: How does an ALU typically evaluate `a == b`?
choices: It computes a − b, discards the result and checks whether the Zero flag is set
It computes a AND b and checks whether the result is all ones
It sends both values to memory and compares their addresses
It uses the NOT operation on both and checks the Carry flag
questions.explain: Comparisons are subtractions whose result is thrown away; only the flags are kept. `a == b` ⇔ a − b = 0 ⇔ Z = 1. Conditional branches like BEQ/JZ then test Z.

questions.q: A simple way to build the 4-operation example ALU is to compute all four results in parallel and choose one. What circuit does the choosing?
choices: A 4-to-1 multiplexer whose 2 select lines are driven by the opcode
A flip-flop that remembers the last opcode
The Control Unit's microcode ROM
The Load-Store Unit
questions.explain: A MUX passes exactly one of its inputs to its output based on its select bits. The opcode drives those select lines, so selection is itself combinational logic.

questions.q: Which gate outputs 1 **only when its two inputs differ**?
choices: XOR
AND
OR
NAND

questions.q: Compute `01100100 AND 00001111`. Answer as 8 binary digits.
questions.explain: Bitwise AND applies the gate to each bit position: a bit is 1 only if both inputs are 1. Masking with `00001111` keeps only the low 4 bits of `01100100`, giving `00000100`.

questions.q: In the standard schematic symbols, which gate is drawn as a triangle with a small circle ("bubble") at its output?
choices: NOT
AND
OR
XOR
questions.explain: NOT = triangle + bubble. AND = flat back, round front. OR = curved back, pointed front. XOR = OR shape with an extra curved line at the input side. A bubble on any output means "inverted" (e.g. NAND, NOR).

questions.q: A half adder adds two bits A and B. What are its outputs?
choices: Sum = A XOR B, Carry = A AND B
Sum = A AND B, Carry = A XOR B
Sum = A OR B, Carry = A AND B
Sum = NOT A, Carry = NOT B
questions.explain: 1 + 1 = binary `10`: sum 0, carry 1. Sum is 1 when exactly one input is 1 (XOR); carry is 1 only when both are (AND). Full adders chain these to form an n-bit ripple-carry adder.

questions.q: Why was two's complement a good choice for representing signed numbers in hardware?
choices: One adder circuit handles addition, subtraction (A + NOT B + 1) and negation
It makes multiplication a single gate
It doubles the range of representable numbers
It removes the need for a Carry flag
questions.explain: Subtraction becomes A + (NOT B) + 1: invert B with XOR gates and set the first carry-in to 1. No separate subtractor is needed.

questions.q: Logic gates are built from transistors, which act as electrically controlled switches.
questions.explain: In CMOS, a NOT gate uses 2 transistors and a NAND uses 4. NAND is universal: any digital circuit can be built from NANDs alone.

questions.q: What does the **Load-Store Unit** handle?
choices: Memory operations during execution: LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP
All memory accesses, including instruction fetch
Arithmetic and logic operations
Decoding instructions into control signals
questions.explain: The LSU moves data between memory (via cache) and registers. These aren't arithmetic, so they don't use the ALU. **Instruction fetch is the exception**: it isn't part of executing an instruction, so the CU handles it.

questions.q: Match each operation to its unit: (i) fetch of the next instruction, (ii) `POP R1`, (iii) `ADD R3, R1, R2`.
choices: (i) CU, (ii) LSU, (iii) ALU
(i) LSU, (ii) LSU, (iii) ALU
(i) CU, (ii) ALU, (iii) ALU
(i) LSU, (ii) CU, (iii) LSU
questions.explain: Fetch → **Control Unit**. PUSH/POP are stores/loads with an automatic stack-pointer update → **LSU**. Register-to-register arithmetic → **ALU**, no memory access.

questions.q: On x86 the stack grows toward lower addresses. What does `PUSH R1` do?
choices: SP ← SP − size, then memory[SP] ← R1
memory[SP] ← R1, then SP ← SP + size
R1 ← memory[SP], then SP ← SP + size
SP ← R1
questions.explain: PUSH decrements the stack pointer and then writes at the new top. POP reads the top and then increments SP. Both are just memory accesses with an address calculation, so the LSU handles them.

questions.q: On a strict **load/store architecture** such as RISC-V, how do you add two numbers stored in memory and save the sum?
choices: LOAD both into registers, ADD the registers, STORE the result
A single ADD instruction with two memory operands
ADD directly in cache, then flush to memory
Ask the Control Unit to add them during fetch
questions.explain: Only loads and stores touch memory; arithmetic is register-only. (x86's `add rax, [rbx]` looks different, but internally it's split into a load micro-op for the LSU and an add micro-op for the ALU.)

questions.q: Which bus carries the READ or WRITE command?
choices: Control bus
Address bus
Data bus
Memory bus
questions.explain: **Address bus** = which location; **data bus** = the value; **control bus** = the command (READ/WRITE) plus clock, interrupt and ready lines.

questions.q: Which statement about bus directions is correct?
choices: The address bus goes out from the CPU; the data bus is bidirectional; control lines go both ways
All three buses are one-way from memory to CPU
The data bus only goes out from the CPU
The address bus is bidirectional so memory can tell the CPU where data is
questions.explain: The CPU (or the unit driving the bus) names the address. Data flows in on a load/fetch and out on a store. Control carries commands out and interrupt/ready signals in.

questions.q: During the execute phase of `STORE R3, [0x208]` (R3 = 12), what appears on the buses? Select all that apply.
choices: `0x208` on the address bus
WRITE on the control bus
`12` on the data bus, going from the CPU to memory
READ on the control bus
The PC's value on the address bus
questions.explain: A store puts the destination address on the address bus, WRITE on the control bus and the value on the data bus (CPU → memory). The PC's value only goes on the address bus during *fetch*.

questions.q: A `LOAD R4, [0x3000]` instruction sits at address `0x0200`. What is on the **address bus** during its fetch and during its execute phase?
choices: Fetch: `0x0200`; execute: `0x3000`
Fetch: `0x3000`; execute: `0x0200`
`0x0200` in both
Fetch: `0x0200`; execute: nothing (loads don't use the bus)
questions.explain: Fetch (CU) sends the PC's value, `0x0200`, with READ; the instruction comes back into the IR. Execute (LSU) sends the data's address, `0x3000`, with READ; the value comes back into R4.

questions.q: The Intel 8086 had 20 address lines. How many bytes could it address, in KiB? (1 KiB = 1,024 bytes)
questions.explain: n address lines → 2^n byte addresses. 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes = 1,024 KiB = 1 MiB.

questions.q: How many bytes does a 64-bit data bus move per transfer?
questions.explain: Data-bus width is bits per transfer: 64 / 8 = 8 bytes.

questions.q: In the worked program (LOAD R1; LOAD R2; ADD R3, R1, R2; STORE R3), how many memory transactions occur in total?
questions.explain: Every instruction is fetched (4 fetches), plus 2 loads and 1 store in execute = **7**. The ADD's execute uses no memory. All those slow memory trips are what motivates cache.

questions.q: After the worked program finishes `LOAD R1,[0x200]` (value 5), `LOAD R2,[0x204]` (value 7), `ADD R3,R1,R2` and `STORE R3,[0x208]` starting at PC = `0x100`, what are the PC and M[0x208]?
questions.explain: Four 4-byte instructions advance the PC from `0x100` to `0x110`. The store writes R3 = 5 + 7 = 12 to `0x208`.

questions.q: The diagram has a thick arrow directly between the CPU and main memory, separate from the system bus. What does it represent in modern systems?
choices: A dedicated high-speed memory bus: the memory controller is built into the CPU and drives DDR channels directly
A wireless link between the CPU and RAM
The PCIe link to the graphics card
The path disks use to reach the CPU
questions.explain: Historically the CPU reached memory through a front-side bus and a northbridge chipset. Today the memory controller is on the CPU die itself.

questions.q: Modern machines mostly replace a single shared set of parallel wires with point-to-point serial links like PCIe, yet the address/data/control model is still the right mental picture.
questions.explain: PCIe lanes connect GPUs, NVMe SSDs and NICs point-to-point. Every transfer still needs an address, data and a command, so the three-bus model still applies conceptually.

questions.q: When can registers update?
choices: Only on a clock edge (tick)
At any time the ALU output changes
Only when the CPU is idle
Only during the decode phase
questions.explain: The clock is a square wave. Logic may change at any time, but edge-triggered registers capture only on the **edge** (e.g. rising, low → high).

questions.q: What is the clock period of a **4 GHz** CPU, in nanoseconds?
What is the clock period of a **3 GHz** CPU, in nanoseconds (to 3 decimal places)?
questions.explain: T = 1 / (3 × 10^9) s ≈ 3.33 × 10^−10 s ≈ **0.333 ns**. In that time light travels only about 10 cm.

questions.q: A 3.5 GHz clock produces how many **billion** potential register updates per second?
questions.explain: GHz = billions of cycles per second, and each cycle is one opportunity for registers to update.

questions.q: What goes wrong if a CPU is overclocked so far that the clock period is shorter than the slowest logic path?
choices: Registers capture values before the logic has settled, causing crashes or silent errors
The CPU automatically executes fewer instructions per cycle but stays correct
The cache is disabled
Nothing; the CPU just gets hotter
questions.explain: The period must exceed the slowest combinational path. Overclockers raise voltage to speed switching, but dynamic power ~ f × V², so heat rises steeply. Overclocking is limited by **stability, heat and power**.

questions.q: A program executes 6 × 10^9 instructions on a 2.5 GHz CPU with CPI = 1. How many seconds does it take?
questions.explain: CPU time = instruction count × CPI / clock rate = 6×10^9 × 1 / 2.5×10^9 = **2.4 s**.

questions.q: CPU X: 3 GHz, CPI = 2. CPU Y: 2.5 GHz, CPI = 1. Both run the same 6 × 10^9-instruction program. Which is faster?
choices: Y (2.4 s vs 4 s)
X (2 s vs 2.4 s)
X, because its clock is faster
They take the same time
questions.explain: X: 6×10^9 × 2 / 3×10^9 = 4 s. Y: 6×10^9 × 1 / 2.5×10^9 = 2.4 s. The lower-GHz chip wins because its CPI is lower: clock speed alone doesn't determine performance.

questions.q: A 4 GHz processor averages 2 cycles per instruction. How many **billion** instructions per second does it execute?
questions.explain: Instructions/s = clock rate / CPI = 4 × 10^9 / 2 = 2 × 10^9.

questions.q: A cache miss that goes all the way to DRAM costs about 100 ns. How many clock cycles is that on a 3 GHz CPU?
questions.explain: 100 ns × 3 cycles/ns = **300 cycles**. This is why cache behaviour dominates CPI in practice.

questions.q: Which properties describe main memory as presented in the module? Select all that apply.
choices: Volatile
Random-access
Organized as a linear array of bytes, each with its own address
Permanent: keeps data after power-off
Located in the I/O subsystem behind a controller
questions.explain: Main memory (RAM) is **temporary/volatile**, **random-access** and a **linear array of bytes**. Permanence and sitting behind a controller in the I/O subsystem describe disk.

questions.q: Why do you lose unsaved work when a program crashes or the power fails?
choices: Unsaved changes live only in volatile main memory; "save" copies them to non-volatile disk
The disk erases recently written files after a crash
The cache writes garbage over the file on disk
The CPU deletes the program's registers from disk
questions.explain: Main memory holds running programs' instructions and data but doesn't retain contents when the program ends, the system crashes or power is removed.

questions.q: Why does DRAM lose its contents without power?
choices: Each bit is charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks, so rows must be refreshed regularly; without power, refresh stops and charge drains
DRAM stores bits magnetically and power keeps the magnets aligned
DRAM is erased by the firmware at every boot
DRAM bits are stored on the CPU die, which resets at power-off
questions.explain: DRAM = one transistor + one capacitor per bit, refreshed at least every 64 ms (JEDEC). SRAM (cache/registers) needs no refresh but still needs power, so it's volatile too.

questions.q: What does "random access" mean?
choices: Any address can be accessed directly without traversing other locations first
Data is stored at random addresses
Reads return a random value if the data isn't cached
The access time varies randomly
questions.explain: The contrast is **sequential access**, like tape, where you must wind past everything before the data you want.

questions.q: Because RAM is random-access, every memory access in a real program takes the same amount of time regardless of access pattern.
questions.explain: RAM has no traversal cost, but real accesses differ: cache hits are ~100× faster than DRAM, open DRAM rows are faster than new ones, and NUMA remote memory is slower. Access patterns can change speed several-fold.

questions.q: A CPU has **16** GPRs of **32 bits** each. How many bytes do they hold in total?
A CPU has **32** GPRs of **64 bits** each. How many bytes do they hold in total?
How many bytes are in 8 GB, using the course's binary definition (1 GB = 2^30 bytes)?
8 GB of RAM (2^33 bytes) is how many times larger than a 64-byte register file? Give the exact number.
16 GB of RAM (binary) versus 32 × 64-bit registers (256 bytes): what is the ratio?
Why don't computers just use registers instead of main memory? Select all that apply.
choices: Registers are much more expensive to produce and take up space directly on the CPU
Registers need more power and generate more heat
A bigger register file would be slower and need more instruction bits to name each register
Registers are non-volatile, so they can't be cleared between programs
Registers can only store instructions, not data
questions.explain: The slides give cost/die space and power/heat. Beyond the slides: bigger register files mean longer wires (slower) and wider register fields in every instruction. Registers are volatile, and GPRs hold data.

questions.q: How many bytes can be addressed with **32-bit** addresses? Answer in GiB.
questions.explain: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 × 2^30 = 4 GiB: the old "4 GB limit" of 32-bit systems.

questions.q: On a little-endian machine, the 4-byte integer `0x12345678` is stored at address `0x1000`. Which byte is at `0x1000`?
questions.explain: Little-endian (x86, most ARM) stores the **least significant byte at the lowest address**: `78 56 34 12` at `0x1000…0x1003`. Big-endian (network byte order) would put `0x12` first.

questions.q: How many bytes are in 1 TB using the course's binary definition? (2^40)
questions.explain: 1 TB = 2^40 = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes (in this course). Unambiguously this is 1 TiB.

questions.q: A drive is sold as **512 GB** (decimal: 512 × 10^9 bytes). About how many GiB (2^30 bytes) does the OS report? Round to 1 decimal place.
questions.explain: 512 × 10^9 / 1,073,741,824 ≈ **476.8 GiB**. Nothing is missing; drive makers use decimal units while OSes (and RAM) use binary.

questions.q: A "256 GB" SSD holds 256 × 10^9 bytes. About how many GiB is that? Round to 1 decimal place.
A network link is rated at **1 Gb/s** (lowercase b). Roughly how many megabytes per second is that?
choices: About 125 MB/s
About 1,000 MB/s
About 8,000 MB/s
About 1 MB/s
questions.explain: Lowercase **b** = bits. 10^9 bits/s ÷ 8 = 1.25 × 10^8 bytes/s ≈ 125 MB/s.

questions.q: "8 GB of RAM" really means how many bytes?
choices: 8 × 2^30 (8 GiB), because memory is always sized in powers of two
questions.explain: RAM comes in power-of-two sizes, so "8 GB of RAM" is 8 GiB = 8,589,934,592 bytes. The decimal convention is what drive makers use.

questions.q: Why does cache improve performance?
choices: It keeps recent/frequently used data close to the CPU so fewer requests go to slower main memory
It makes the clock run faster
It stores data permanently so it survives power-off
It lets the ALU skip the decode phase
questions.explain: Every trip to main memory is a delay. Cache (small, fast, in or near the CPU) satisfies most requests without that trip. It is volatile, like RAM.

questions.q: Which statement about L1, L2 and L3 is correct?
choices: L1 is the smallest and fastest; L3 is the largest and slowest (and typically shared by all cores)
L3 is the smallest and fastest
All three levels are the same size but differ in speed
L1 is shared by all cores; L3 is private to each core
questions.explain: Each tier is progressively larger and slower: L1 (tens of KB per core, ~1 ns), L2 (MB per core), L3 (8-100+ MB per chip, shared).

questions.q: Cache memory is non-volatile, unlike main memory.
questions.explain: Like main memory, cache is **temporary and volatile**. It is built from SRAM, which needs power to hold state.

questions.q: Roughly how does total cache in consumer devices (20-60 MB) compare to main memory (~9 billion to ~2 trillion bytes)?
choices: Main memory is roughly 140 to 100,000 times larger
They are about the same size
Cache is larger
Main memory is about 2-3 times larger
questions.explain: 8,589,934,592 / 62,914,560 ≈ 137 at the low end, and 2^41 / 20,971,520 ≈ 104,858 at the high end. Because cache is so small it must be managed effectively.

questions.q: What happens on a **cache miss**?
choices: The request goes to the next level down (eventually main memory), and the fetched data is brought into cache so the next access hits
The CPU raises an error and the program stops
The ALU recomputes the value
The data is read from disk directly into the register
questions.explain: A hit returns quickly (L1 ~1 ns). A miss goes down the hierarchy (DRAM ~100 ns) and fills the cache on the way back.

questions.q: A program reads **1 byte** that isn't in cache on a current x86-64 CPU. How much data is brought into cache?
choices: A whole 64-byte cache line containing that byte
Exactly 1 byte
One 4 KB page
The entire array the byte belongs to
questions.explain: Caches transfer fixed-size **cache lines** (64 bytes on x86-64). Loading neighbours along with the requested byte is what exploits spatial locality.

questions.q: A loop's running total `sum` is read and written on every iteration. Which kind of locality does this show?
choices: Temporal locality
Spatial locality
Sequential access
No locality
questions.explain: **Temporal**: data used recently is likely to be used again soon. Stepping to the next array element would be **spatial** locality (nearby data).

questions.q: A loop walks through consecutive elements `a[0], a[1], a[2], …`. Which kind of locality does this mainly exploit?
choices: Spatial locality
Temporal locality
Random access
Reset locality
questions.explain: **Spatial**: data near recently used data is likely to be used soon. Each 64-byte line brought in supplies 16 consecutive ints.

questions.q:
In C, a 2-D array is stored row by row. Which loop is cache-friendly for large N?

(A) `for i … for j … sum += a[i][j];`
(B) `for j … for i … sum += a[i][j];`
choices: (A), because it walks memory sequentially, using every byte of each cache line
(B), because it visits each column once
Both are equally fast because RAM is random-access
(B), because it has fewer iterations
questions.explain: (A) steps through consecutive addresses (spatial locality). (B) jumps a whole row (N × 4 bytes) between accesses, so for large N nearly every access misses and waits ~100 ns. Same arithmetic, several times slower. This is what "poor cache management can tank performance" means for programmers.

questions.q: When the cache is full and a new line must be loaded, what typically decides which line is evicted?
choices: A replacement policy, usually an approximation of least recently used (LRU)
The line with the lowest address
A random line chosen by the OS
The line holding the PC's value
questions.explain: LRU exploits temporal locality: the line not used for the longest time is the least likely to be needed soon.

questions.q: Why is L1 cache commonly split into L1i and L1d?
choices: So instruction fetch (L1i) and the LSU's data accesses (L1d) can proceed at the same time
Because instructions are larger than data
Because L1d is non-volatile
So the OS can encrypt instructions separately
questions.explain: This is the Harvard-like part of a "modified Harvard" design: separate fast paths for instructions and data avoid contention at the top of the hierarchy.

questions.q: Order these from fastest/smallest to slowest/largest: main memory, L1 cache, SSD, registers, L3 cache.
choices: Registers, L1, L3, main memory, SSD
L1, registers, L3, SSD, main memory
Registers, L3, L1, main memory, SSD
Main memory, registers, L1, L3, SSD
questions.explain: Registers (<1 ns) → L1 (~1 ns) → L2/L3 (~4-40 ns) → DRAM (~100 ns) → SSD (~0.1 ms) / HDD (~10 ms). Going down: larger, slower, cheaper per byte; only disk is non-volatile.

questions.q: What single trade-off explains why computers stack registers, cache, RAM and disk?
choices: No storage is fast, large and cheap all at once, so small fast layers hold the most-used data and large cheap layers hold the rest
Faster storage is always larger, so fewer layers are needed
Every program requires exactly four kinds of storage
Disks can only talk to RAM, and RAM can only talk to cache
questions.explain: The fast ↔ large ↔ cheap trade-off. Locality lets the hierarchy give close to top-level speed at close to bottom-level cost. Module 3 develops this.

questions.q: Why is a laptop's **integrated** graphics adapter considered an I/O device even though it's on the CPU package?
choices: "I/O" is about function, not location: it produces output for a display and is accessed through a device interface, not as part of the CU/ALU/registers
It isn't; integrated graphics are part of the CPU
Because it is connected by USB
Because it stores data permanently
questions.explain: The slides stress that I/O does not mean "external". Integrated graphics and the built-in NIC are treated by the machine as I/O devices.

questions.q: Which of these devices do **both** input and output? Select all that apply.
choices: Touchscreen
Network card
Headset (mic + speakers)
Keyboard
Monitor
questions.explain: A touchscreen displays and senses touch; a NIC sends and receives; a headset has mic (in) and speakers (out). A keyboard is input only and a monitor is output only.

questions.q: Why does the CPU communicate with devices through **controllers**?
choices: Controllers provide an abstraction: the CPU only needs to know *what* to tell a device, not *how* the device works
Controllers make devices run faster than the CPU
The CPU has no address bus
Controllers store the device's data permanently
questions.explain: Like calling a function without knowing its implementation. The disk controller exposes "read block 1,000" and hides whether that means moving a head over a platter (HDD) or reading flash (SSD).

questions.q: How do the graphics adapter and NIC differ from the USB controller in the module's diagram?
choices: They are both the I/O device and its own controller; the USB controller is a separate controller managing many different devices
They connect directly to the CPU without the system bus
They are not I/O devices
They use the LSU instead of a controller
questions.explain: Graphics adapter → display and NIC → network each appear as one box on the bus. The USB controller manages keyboards, mice, flash drives, webcams and so on plugged into it.

questions.q: What is a **device driver**?
choices: OS software that knows a specific controller's registers and protocol and presents a generic interface to the rest of the OS
The firmware that runs at the reset vector
A hardware chip that replaces the controller
The cable connecting a device to the bus
questions.explain: Layers: application → OS generic interface → driver → controller → device. Each layer only needs to know the one directly below, the same layered idea as network protocol stacks.

questions.q: With **memory-mapped I/O**, how does the CPU write a command to a device register?
choices: An ordinary STORE to an address assigned to the device register, through the LSU and the usual buses
A special x86 `out` instruction to a separate I/O address space
By writing the command to disk and rebooting
By changing the reset vector
questions.explain: Device registers get ordinary memory addresses, so normal loads and stores reach the device instead of RAM. The special-instruction approach is **port-mapped** I/O. Memory-mapped is dominant today.

questions.q: What is the advantage of **interrupts** over **polling**?
choices: The CPU can do other work instead of repeatedly checking a status register; the device signals when it's done
Interrupts never require the OS to run any code
Polling can't read device registers
Interrupts make the device itself faster
questions.explain: Polling wastes CPU time spinning on the status register. With interrupts the device raises a signal on a control line; the CPU saves state, runs the OS interrupt handler, then resumes.

questions.q: What does **DMA** do?
choices: Lets a device copy bulk data directly to or from main memory without the CPU moving each word; the CPU is interrupted when the transfer finishes
Doubles the memory bandwidth by using two buses
Moves data directly between registers and disk, skipping RAM
Makes the CPU fetch instructions from the device
questions.explain: Direct Memory Access frees the CPU during disk-block or network-packet transfers.

questions.q: You press a key. Which path best describes what happens?
choices: The USB controller receives it and interrupts the CPU; the OS driver reads the key code
The keyboard writes the key directly into a CPU register
The graphics adapter reads the keyboard and sends the key to RAM
The disk controller stores the key and the CPU polls the disk
questions.explain: Keyboard → USB controller → interrupt on a control line → OS interrupt handler / driver reads the code over the bus.

questions.q: What does a NIC do with an **incoming** frame?
choices: Receives the signals, reassembles and error-checks the frame and places it in main memory for the OS
Executes it as an instruction
Sends it directly to the display
Stores it permanently on the NIC
questions.explain: Outgoing, it converts OS-prepared frames to electrical/radio signals; incoming, it does the reverse and hands frames to memory (often by DMA). Each NIC has a 48-bit **MAC address**.

questions.q: When you plug a device into USB, the controller and OS perform **enumeration**. What does that achieve?
choices: The device is reset, given an address, and its descriptors are read so the right driver can be loaded
The device's firmware is erased and rewritten
The CPU's reset vector is changed to the device
The device is mounted as main memory
questions.explain: Descriptors say "I am a keyboard" or "I am mass storage", so the OS knows which driver to use.

questions.q: What distinguishes secondary storage (disk memory) from main memory?
choices: It is permanent and non-volatile, surviving program termination, crashes and power-off
It is faster than main memory
The CPU executes instructions directly from it
It is located inside the CPU
questions.explain: Disk is permanent and non-volatile but slower (and cheaper per byte) than RAM. It sits in the I/O subsystem behind a disk controller.

questions.q: The CPU can fetch and execute instructions directly from disk without copying them to main memory.
questions.explain: Programs must be loaded from disk into main memory first; the fetch step reads from main memory (via cache). Disk is an I/O device behind a controller.

questions.q: How does an SSD store data, compared with an HDD?
choices: SSD: trapped electrical charge in NAND flash cells, no moving parts; HDD: magnetic regions on spinning platters
SSD: magnetic platters; HDD: flash cells
Both store charge on capacitors that need refresh
SSD stores data in RAM backed by a battery
questions.explain: Flash cells trap electrons in an insulated floating gate or charge trap, so data stays without power. HDDs move a head over spinning magnetic platters.

questions.q: A 7,200 RPM disk: what is the **average** rotational latency, in milliseconds (half a rotation)? Round to 2 decimals.
questions.explain: One rotation = 60 s / 7,200 = 8.33 ms. On average you wait half a rotation: ≈ **4.17 ms**. Add ~5 ms seek and a random read costs ~10 ms, about 100,000× DRAM's ~100 ns.

questions.q: Why do SSDs use **wear leveling**?
choices: Each program/erase cycle damages the cell's insulation, so the controller spreads writes evenly to keep any cell from wearing out early
To keep the platters balanced while spinning
To refresh cells before their charge leaks away every 64 ms
To make reads faster than writes
questions.explain: Cells endure roughly 100,000 cycles (SLC) down to about 1,000 (TLC/QLC). Wear leveling runs in the SSD controller's own firmware.

questions.q: What is a **virtual hard disk**?
choices: Software-defined storage, such as a file on the host (.vhdx, .vmdk, .qcow2) or a network volume, presented to a VM as a disk
An SSD with no controller
A RAM disk that loses data at shutdown
The portion of an HDD reserved for the OS
questions.explain: The guest OS sees an ordinary disk; the hypervisor turns its reads/writes into operations on the file or network block volume (e.g. AWS EBS).

questions.q: How many bytes is 4 TB in the course's binary units? (4 × 2^40)
About how much faster is a random read from an SSD (~0.1 ms) than from an HDD (~10 ms)?
choices: About 100×
About 2×
About 10,000×
They're the same
questions.explain: 10 ms / 0.1 ms = 100. Both are still vastly slower than DRAM (~100 ns).

questions.q: Why are NVMe SSDs lower-latency than SATA drives using AHCI?
choices: NVMe runs over PCIe with up to 64K queues of 64K commands, while AHCI was designed for HDDs with one 32-command queue
NVMe drives use magnetic platters that spin faster
AHCI drives are connected by USB
NVMe drives are part of main memory
questions.explain: AHCI's single shallow queue suited slow HDDs. NVMe's many deep queues over PCIe match flash's parallelism.

questions.q: In the "putting it all together" story, what does saving a document physically do?
choices: Copies data from volatile main memory, through the disk controller over the bus, to non-volatile disk
Moves the document from cache into registers
Marks the RAM pages as permanent
Sends the document to the graphics adapter
questions.explain: Save = copy from memory (volatile) to disk (non-volatile) so the data survives a crash or power-off.
